content: Red blood cell alloimmunization during pregnancy can result in fetal anemia, which may have severe and potentially life-threatening consequences. The traditional approach to managing this condition involves intrauterine transfusion, a procedure that carries significant risks related to its invasive nature. An alternative treatment that has been explored is the administration of immunoglobulin intravenously to the pregnant mother. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of antenatal intravenous immunoglobulin therapy for women experiencing severe fetal red blood cell alloimmunization. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group trials register as of December 19, 2012, along with a review of reference lists from relevant articles. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that investigated the use of intravenous immunoglobulin during pregnancy, regardless of the dose, frequency, or duration, compared to any other treatment or no treatment at all, in the context of managing fetal red blood cell alloimmunization. Two independent reviewers assessed the available evidence. However, no randomized controlled trials meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. As a result, there is no evidence from randomized trials to determine whether antenatal intravenous immunoglobulin is effective in managing fetal red blood cell alloimmunization. Nonetheless, findings from several case series suggest that this treatment may have a beneficial role in delaying the onset of fetal anemia, potentially reducing the need for invasive intrauterine transfusion.
